extracted.intended_audience: Parliamentarians, lawmakers, and the learned public (authors, printers, clergy, and intellectuals)
extracted.subtask_description: A polemic arguing against state licensing/censorship of printed works, addressing the practical, moral, and intellectual consequences of imposing an Imprimatur. It evaluates the effects on learning, authorship, governance, and public virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms_justifying_censorship_must_be_real_and_specific
rubrics_metrics.description: The ostensible harms (the 'infection' books may spread) are the usual ground for licensing—books feared to taint life and doctrine are cited as cause for suppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues this justification is overbroad and often false: many great works (even the Bible and the Fathers) contain passages that could be misread or offensive, yet are indispensable to learning; the mere possibility of misinterpretation does not warrant wholesale suppression. Examples: Bible passages that could be read as blasphemous or the Fathers appearing to teach heresies; classical ribaldry accessible to courtiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness_of_licensing_vs_oral_and_social_transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: If the aim is to prevent the spread of vice or heresy through books, licensing is ineffective because learned men and social networks can transmit corrupting ideas orally or by other non-printed means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books are not the only vectors of corruption; learned people transmit ideas to princes and the populace, and dangerous doctrines can spread without print. Licensing thus cannot fully achieve its end; attempts to do so would be vain and impossible (compares to trying to 'pound up the crows by shutting his park gate').

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity_of_competent_infallible_licensers
rubrics_metrics.description: To entrust censorship to licensers presupposes their infallibility and incorruptibility; otherwise the appointment is dangerous and unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensers would need to be 'above the common measure, both studious, learned, and judicious.' In practice, the office is tedious and will be filled by the unwilling, ignorant, imperious, remiss, or pecuniary-minded, leading to mistakes, injustice, and arbitrary suppression. Example: present licensers already complain of the burden, indicating the role's unattractiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative_burden_and_scope_expand_beyond_print
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulating printed books would logically require regulating all other forms of recreation, speech, and cultural expression to be consistent and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one seeks to 'rectify manners' by regulating printing, one must also license music, dance, clothes, conversation, household entertainments, and even fiddlers' ballads—an impossible, absurd expansion. The author lists lutes, violins, madrigals, windows, balconies, and village bagpipes as examples of domains that would be implicated, demonstrating impracticability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing_discourages_learning_and_authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: An order of licensing is the greatest discouragement and affront to learning and learned men, diminishing incentive to study and publish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposing a perpetual overseer (an Imprimatur) reduces authors to 'pupil teachers' under guardianship, dishonors their work, and deters diligent writers. Practical harms include: inability to add late improvements (printer cannot go beyond licensed copy), authors forced to seek licenser repeatedly, and reputational damage when a licenser's hand is stamped on a title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing_can_remove_amount_of_virtue_with_vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to remove the matter of sin (books/objects) will also remove the matter of virtue, because the same materials enable both vice and virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing objects or restricting access does not change dispositions; it may expel sources of virtue along with vice. Example: banishing all objects of lust and shutting youth into hermitages would not make them chaste if their dispositions are unchanged. Therefore, a law that indiscriminately abridges means is frivolous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain_works_require_guidance_rather_than_suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Books of religious controversy and complex theological works are often not understood without a guide and so are less likely to seduce the ignorant on their own; suppression of such works is misguided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contends it's hard to point to an ignorant person seduced by an English papistical book unless it was recommended or explained by clergy. Controversial treatises act like Isaiah's prophecy to the eunuch—not to be 'UNDERSTOOD WITHOUT A GUIDE'—so permitting them while educating readers is preferable to prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing_requires_extensive_and_unending_curation
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent harmful publications, a licensing regime would need ongoing, resource-intensive tasks: listing condemned books, expurgating mixed works, examining foreign books, and cataloguing offending printers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an office would occupy many overseers and require continual labour; even then, it would be incomplete. The author compares necessary reform to the models of Trent and Seville—systems the readership supposedly abhors—showing that a thorough censorship apparatus would be authoritarian and foreign to England's values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing_leads_to_error_and_loss_of_valuable_thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensers' mistakes or timorousness can suppress valuable or daring utterances, even from celebrated authors, causing permanent loss to posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single 'venturous' sentence in a deceased or living author's work could be struck out by a 'perfunctory licenser,' erasing important insights; examples mention Knox and Galileo to show high-profile victimization. This is a treacherous fraud against the memory and labours of the dead and living.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship_fosters_hypocrisy_and_delegation_of_religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensing treats the public as incapable of exercising religious judgment, promoting a culture of delegated, transactional religion where people outsource their conscience to a visible authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author observes Protestants who live in implicit faith by adhering to a single divine or pastor as a 'factor' for their religion; a licensing regime exacerbates this tendency by implying the laity cannot be trusted with religious reading. This is presented as a social and spiritual harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment_and_forbidding_increase_authority_and_nurse_sects
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribing books often enhances their prestige and fuels sectarianism rather than suppressing dissent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites the view that forbidden writings are taken for sparks of truth and that punishing wits 'enhances their authority' (Viscount St. Albans). Thus censorship can be a 'nursing-mother to sects' and a 'step-dame to Truth.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer_education_persuasion_over_compulsion_in_moral_regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: To govern morals and learning wisely, a state should emphasize virtuous education, religious and civil nurture, and persuasion rather than coercive licensing and punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's rigid licensing is criticized as inapplicable; the author endorses 'unwritten' laws of virtuous education and the 'grave and governing wisdom of a state' to discern where law should restrain and where persuasion should operate. This is presented as a constructive alternative to licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing_reflects_mistrust_and_disgrace_to_authors_and_nation
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposing licensers on all writers implies a deep mistrust of authors and devalues national learning, reducing the nation's intellectual work to a commodity needing stamps and tickets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that treating truth and understanding as wares to be monopolized is servitude; it is an 'undervaluing and vilifying of the whole nation.' This criterion condemns licensing as insulting to both authors and the public.
